TauLang: A Language and Compiler for Space-Time
Programming on Statically Scheduled Accelerators
Xuxiao Yang1, Junchi Wu1, Yuqi Peng2, Feiyang Wu1, Zhuoran Li1, Wei Kong2, Shuo Tao2, Dongyi
Fan2, Yiming Zhang2, Keqin Luo2, Xingrui Gao2, Hao Zhang 2, Xuehai Qian2, Youwei Zhuo1
1School of Integrated Circuits, Peking University Beijing China
2Tsinghua University Beijing China
{valinor, 2501111908}@stu.pku.edu.cn, pyq24@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn, {fywu25, zhuoranli}@stu.pku.edu.cn, {kongw24,
taos23, fdy24, zym24, luokq24, gxr24, hao-zhang}@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn, xuehaiq@tsinghua.edu.cn,
youwei@pku.edu.cn
Abstract
Statically scheduled accelerators such as Groq’s Tensor Stream-
ing Processor (TSP) achieve low-latency large language model
inference by stripping dynamic synchronization hardware
from the chip. With no caches, arbiters, or hardware sched-
ulers, the compiler must fix the exact slice and issue cycle
of every operation, so when an operation runs is a condi-
tion for correctness. Existing kernel languages cannot target
such machines because they rely on hardware to resolve
cycle timing and instead encode schedules implicitly in code
structure.
We present TauLang, a kernel language and compiler that
makes time a first-class citizen of the program. The pro-
grammer schedules operations, loops, and composed ker-
nels with parameterized explicit times, so exploring sched-
ules means changing parameter values rather than rewriting
code. TauLang validates explicit times algebraically in TauIR,
its timed intermediate representation. It then solves tensor
placement and cycle scheduling jointly in an integer linear
program, using explicit times to group connected operations
into timing clusters that prune the search space. On a cycle-
accurate model of a TSP-like machine, joint search achieves
a 1.40× latency speedup across ten kernels over a space-first
flow. A few explicit time pins keep latency within one cy-
cle of the untimed schedules and scale joint search to 1,636
GEMM blocks, whereas untimed search finds no schedule at
32.
1
Introduction
Statically scheduled accelerators, pioneered by Groq’s Tensor
Streaming Processor (TSP) [1, 2], have emerged as a com-
pelling architecture for low-latency large language model
inference. Reflecting this demand for fast token generation,
Nvidia recently acquired Groq’s assets for $20 billion [9] and
introduced a rack-scale system built on the TSP execution
model [3]. To achieve such low, deterministic latency, this
execution model strips out the dynamic control hardware of
conventional accelerators, eliminating caches, local register
files, interconnect arbiters, and hardware schedulers [36].
However, the simplicity of the hardware makes compi-
lation harder. With no stall signals or runtime handshakes,

Instruction flow
Figure 1. (a) Instructions flow vertically while data streams
horizontally across slices. (b) Staggered loads make data
𝑎0,𝑏0 and the add instruction meet at VXM in the same cycle.
instructions flow vertically up each slice while data streams
move horizontally across functional units at a fixed rate of
one slice per cycle, without waiting (Figure 1a). Thus, the
compiler must statically decide the exact slice and issue cy-
cle of every operation so that each instruction and its input
streams meet at the target unit in the exact same cycle (Fig-
ure 1b), while avoiding conflicts on shared stream register
(SR) tracks and memory banks. Because the hardware de-
tects no timing or resource violations, missing a rendezvous
by even one cycle or slice silently produces wrong results,
which makes when an operation runs a condition for cor-
rectness rather than a performance parameter. Moreover, a
single chip contains dozens of slices, so the compiler must
coordinate these cycle-exact schedules across all slices and
functional units simultaneously.
Existing approaches to this challenge fall between two
extremes. On one hand, expert engineers can hand-craft low-
level instruction schedules [1, 36], but doing so demands
painstaking cycle-level control and months of effort. For ex-
ample, after Groq initially brought up Llama-2 70B at 100 to-
kens/s, its engineers spent three months optimizing low-level
schedules on the same hardware to reach 300 tokens/s [13].
On the other hand, a compiler that schedules high-level code
automatically faces a vast joint space of slice placements
and issue cycles. Fixing placement first shrinks this space
but yields slower schedules, whereas in our experiments, an
unconstrained solver finds no schedule for a 32-block GEMM
within the time budget. A natural middle ground is a kernel
1

--- Page 2 ---
Xuxiao Yang, Junchi Wu, Yuqi Peng, Feiyang Wu, Zhuoran Li, Wei Kong, Shuo Tao, Dongyi Fan, Yiming Zhang, Keqin Luo, Xingrui Gao, Hao Zhang, Xuehai
Qian, and Youwei Zhuo
language that lets the programmer express high-level sched-
uling decisions while the compiler checks and completes the
low-level schedule.
However, neither GPU kernel languages [37, 39] nor spa-
tial compilers [23–25] can serve as this middle ground, be-
cause they assume that hardware synchronizes timing at run-
time. Even compilers for spatial meshes and coarse-grained
reconfigurable arrays (CGRAs) that plan placement and mod-
ulo cycles statically [23–25] rely on scratchpads, FIFOs, and
router flow control to buffer early arrivals [12, 34], so a
one-cycle mismatch costs only throughput. Under this as-
sumption, existing kernel languages are time-blind and in-
stead express schedules indirectly through code structure,
such as pipeline stage counts and explicit barriers (Figure 2).
This structural approach neither expresses cycle-exact ren-
dezvous nor separates the schedule from the abstract syntax
tree (AST), so the programmer must rewrite the kernel to
change its schedule.
Our key insight is to decouple a program’s schedule from
its code structure by making time a first-class citizen of
the kernel language. Because cycle timing determines cor-
rectness on a statically scheduled accelerator, the language
should let the programmer express cycle times directly and
the compiler check them statically (Figure 3). Programmers
write explicit times as affine cycle expressions over loop in-
dices and kernel parameters, and pinning a kernel call to an
invocation time offsets every explicit time in the callee. Ex-
ploring schedules across a composed program thus requires
only changing parameter values rather than rewriting the
kernel. Pins also keep the compiler’s joint search over the
remaining schedule tractable. Because streams advance one
slice per cycle, pinning the cycle gap between a stream’s
producer and consumer fixes the hop count between their
slices, which prunes the memory placements that the solver
must explore.
We present TauLang, a kernel language and compiler for
statically scheduled accelerators. TauLang extends a tile-
style Python DSL with explicit times relative to symbolic
times, which mark the start of the current kernel (tau.T) or
the start or end of an operation, loop, or call (tau.start,
tau.end). A pin (.at) fixes the issue time of an operation
or the invocation time of a call, while tau.domain maps
each loop iteration to its start cycle. The compiler lowers
explicit times into TauIR attributes in MLIR [21] and runs
affine time validation to catch timing conflicts algebraically
before search. It then solves spatial placement and cycle
scheduling jointly as an integer linear program (ILP), using
stream dependences and explicit times to group connected
operations into timing clusters that prune the search.
We evaluate TauLang on a TSP-like machine using a cycle-
accurate simulator validated against our SystemVerilog RTL
implementation. Across ten kernels from BLAS, PolyBench,
ResNet, and Transformer layers at three sizes each, joint
search achieves a 1.40× geometric-mean latency speedup
(up to 2.22×) over the space-first flow, which fixes placement
before scheduling greedily. Adding one to three pins per
kernel matches untimed latency within one cycle and cuts
compile time by 1.72×. Pins also scale joint search to 1,636
GEMM blocks and 128 residual blocks, whereas untimed
search finds no schedule at 32 and 8. Sweeping two schedule
parameters of a flow-matching kernel yields eight Pareto-
optimal schedules among those compiled, which trade up to
237 cycles of first-item latency for 498 cycles of whole-output
time.
This paper makes three contributions.
• A time-first kernel language. We design TauLang,
to our knowledge the first kernel language that treats
cycle time as a first-class, parameterized, and compos-
able construct (§4).
• A timed intermediate representation. We define
TauIR, an IR that carries symbolic timing attributes
and validates them algebraically before scheduling
(§5).
• Time-guided joint space-time scheduling. We for-
mulate placement and scheduling as a joint ILP that
uses explicit times to group operations into timing
clusters and prune the search space (§6).
2
Background and Motivating Examples
2.1
The TSP Execution Model
Groq’s TSP [1, 2] is the most widely deployed statically sched-
uled accelerator, so we use it as our target architecture. On
the row of slices in Figure 1a, instructions step vertically up
each slice across its lanes while values travel east or west on
SR tracks at one slice per cycle. Memory slices (MEM) store
tensors in SRAM banks, vector (VXM) and switch (SXM) slices
perform arithmetic and lane permutations, and matrix slices
(MXM) hold weights across two planes so one plane can in-
stall weights while the other computes. Because execution
and stream propagation are deterministic, a consumer sees a
producer’s output at a fixed cycle. An operation samples its
operands 𝑑skew cycles after it issues and writes its result to
an SR 𝑑func cycles after it issues. Let 𝛿be the hop count from
producer 𝑃to consumer 𝐶. 𝐶receives 𝑃’s value if and only if
𝑡issue(𝑃) + 𝑑func(𝑃) + 1 + 𝛿= 𝑡issue(𝐶) + 𝑑skew(𝐶).
(1)
Figure 1b illustrates this rendezvous for 𝑐= 𝑎+𝑏, where MEM
W1 is one slice farther from VXM than MEM W0 and therefore
issues its load of 𝑎one cycle earlier so that 𝑎0 and 𝑏0 reach
add on VXM in the same cycle. Furthermore, at most one
producer may write a given SR track at any slice and cycle,
and each memory bank serves at most one access per cycle.
The hardware detects neither violation and silently produces
wrong values instead.

        T.gemm(A_shared, B_shared, C_local)
        T.barrier_arrive(compute_is_done)

2.2
Schedules in Existing Kernel Languages
Because the best schedule of a kernel varies across workloads,
the programmer needs fine-grained control over when each
operation executes. On a statically scheduled machine, this
schedule also determines correctness, as every operand must
arrive at the exact slice and cycle its instruction expects.
We examine how TileLang [39] expresses the schedule of a
GEMM and why that schedule does not carry over to the
TSP.
TileLang describes a kernel as an iteration domain whose
body applies tile operators such as load, store, and matrix
multiply to whole tiles [39]. In the pipelined GEMM in Fig-
ure 2, T.Pipelined specifies a stage count ➊to overlap iter-
ations through multi-buffered copies, while runtime barriers
synchronize stages ➋as each multiply waits for its copies
and each pair of copies waits for the previous multiply.1
Thus, the loop runs at whatever pace the copies and bar-
riers deliver at runtime. Both constructs rely on hardware
synchronization, where copies signal completion and barri-
ers stall waiting warps. On the TSP, nothing waits, because
a consumer receives a value only in the cycle required by
Equation 1.
As this GEMM shows, existing kernel languages share
two limitations. First, they cannot express cycle timing, so
the programmer cannot specify even the initiation interval
of a loop. Second, the control they do expose is coarse and
written in the structure of the code, so another schedule is
another program. For instance, alongside the kernel in Fig-
ure 2, TileLang provides a separate program to swap which
warp group copies tiles and which performs matrix multipli-
cation. Both limitations arise because time is not a first-class
citizen of these languages. TauLang addresses both by keep-
ing the loops and tile operators of a tile-style language and
adding explicit times, cycle counts written over ordinary ker-
nel parameters, so another schedule is simply another set
of parameter values on the same program. Sections 2.3–2.5
preview through concrete examples how explicit times pa-
rameterize schedules, enable static timing checks, and prune
placement and scheduling.
1The code listings in this section omit type annotations, explicit casts, and
routine implementation details.
@jit
def tile(A, B, S, k, M, KB, II, H):
    for i in tau.domain(M, at=lambda i: tau.T + i * II):
        a = load(A, addr=i * KB + k)
        d = tau.dot(a, B[k]).at(tau.start(a) + H + DOT)
        store(S, load(S, addr=i) + d, addr=i)
@jit
def matmul(A, B, S, C, M, KB, P, II, L, H):
    tiles = tau.domain(KB, at=lambda k: tau.T + k * P)
    for k in tiles:
        tile(A, B, S, k, M, KB, II, H).at(tiles[k] + L)
    for i in tau.domain(M, at=lambda i: tau.end(tiles) + i * II):
        store(C, load(S, addr=i), addr=i)

2.3
Explicit Times in a Tiled GEMM
Figure 3 writes the same tiled GEMM in TauLang, where
matmul calls tile on each block along 𝐾to install weights
on an MXM plane and stream rows of 𝐴. Rather than encoding
the schedule in stage counts and barriers, TauLang states
loop strides directly in cycles with tau.domain and fixes
selected stage offsets with .at. Inside tile, the row domain
(➊) starts a new row of 𝐴every II cycles, and .at pins the
accumulation at 𝐻+ DOT cycles after load(A), where 𝐻is
the hop count from load(A) to the matrix unit. In matmul,
the tiles domain (➋) starts a new block of 𝐵every 𝑃cycles
and leaves 𝐿cycles to install weights before calling tile.
The final loop drains the partial sums 𝑆to 𝐶once the last
tile finishes.
Because 𝑃and II are ordinary kernel parameters, exploring
schedules reduces to changing parameter values on the same
code (Figure 4). A large tile stride runs the three tiles sequen-
tially, waiting for one tile’s rows to finish before installing
the next weight block (Figure 4a). Shortening 𝑃pipelines ad-
jacent tiles across the two MXM planes so each weight install
overlaps the previous tile’s rows (Figure 4b), while raising II
spaces rows apart to free cycles for another kernel running

2.4
Checking Explicit Times
Because explicit times directly control when operations issue,
an invalid schedule can violate data dependences. Suppose
the programmer extends the GEMM across column blocks
of 𝐵and starts the final loop early to overlap it with the tile
walk. If the final loop drains columns faster than the walk
finishes accumulating them, later columns read elements of
𝑆before their last write. Whereas a GPU barrier would stall
such a read until the write completes, the TSP reads the stale
partial sum from SRAM and silently corrupts 𝐶. TauLang
rejects the program before scheduling with a read-before-
write error on 𝑆that cites the offending source lines, and
accepts it once each column of the final loop starts after its
tile walk finishes (§5.2).
2.5
Pinning One Stage in Attention
Pins are optional, so in a loop body where multiple streams
reconverge, the programmer pins only the stages of interest.
Figure 5 shows such a body in the softmax pass of a three-
pass attention kernel, after pass 1 has computed the scores
𝑆and the row maxima 𝑀. The pass iterates over the KT
key tiles in a plain range loop, while the inner tau.domain
schedules both loops by incorporating the outer index 𝑘into
its time map (➊). Each row computes 𝑒= exp(𝑆−𝑀), stores
it to 𝐸, and adds its cross-lane sum tile_sum_f16(e) to the
running denominator in 𝑍. By Equation 1, the scores and
the row maximum must reach sub_f32 in the same cycle,
as must the row sum and the denominator loaded from 𝑍at
add_f32.
The .at call (➋) pins exp_f32 EXP cycles after its row
starts. Because the time map fixes the row start, the pin
fixes every cycle gap along the path from the loads of 𝑆and
𝑀through sub_f32 to exp_f32. Beyond fixing that timing,
the pin turns the path into one timing cluster whose cycle
gaps and hop counts the solver no longer searches, which is
how pins cut compile time in §8.4. The reduction tail after
exp_f32 carries no explicit time, and the compiler places
and schedules the row sum, the load of 𝑍, and add_f32 so
that their operands arrive in the same cycle.

Figure 6. The TauLang workflow, from the DSL to the sched-
uled TauIR. Each explicit time remains an attribute of the call,
loop, or operation it schedules until placement and schedul-
ing assign slices and issue cycles.
Figure 6 shows how TauLang compiles a kernel written
with explicit timing constructs (§4) into one timestamped
program per slice. An IR builder pass first captures the ker-
nel into TauIR (§5). As the captured TauIR box illustrates,
each call carries an invocation_time, each timed loop car-
ries a start_time, and each pinned operation carries an
issue_time. Before any slice or cycle is assigned, validation
passes check these attributes algebraically for timing errors
that are independent of placement, such as the overlapped
final loop of §2.4.
Placement and scheduling then run in one of two flows
(§6) to assign slices and issue cycles for all operations while
satisfying Equation 1 and every explicit time. The cluster
flow, our third contribution, formulates joint search as an ILP
that decides where each tensor buffer resides in memory and
when every operation issues. To keep this search tractable,
the flow first merges operations whose cycle gaps are fixed
into timing clusters. The space-first flow serves as a fast
4


--- Page 5 ---
TauLang: A Language and Compiler for Space-Time Programming on Statically Scheduled Accelerators
baseline that assigns slices using deterministic rules and
then schedules issue cycles greedily. Both flows emit the
scheduled TauIR at the bottom of the figure, which lists
each operation on its assigned slice with its issue cycle. Code
generation then assembles the scheduled TauIR into per-slice
instruction streams (§7).
4
The TauLang Language
As previewed in §2.3 and §2.5, TauLang extends a tile-style
Python DSL with explicit times, which the programmer spec-
ifies where timing matters while the compiler schedules the
rest. Every explicit time is an affine cycle offset from a sym-
bolic root over the enclosing loop indices and compile-time
kernel parameters. Symbolic times supply the roots, pins
attach a time to an operation or a call, and iteration domains
attach a time map to a loop.
4.1
Symbolic Times
Absolute cycle numbers from the start of the program would
break modularity whenever a sub-kernel is reused or pre-
ceded by other stages. Instead, every explicit time is an offset
from one of three symbolic times, tau.T, tau.start, and
tau.end. tau.T denotes the start of the current kernel invo-
cation. tau.start(x) and tau.end(x) return the symbolic
time at which an operation, iteration domain, or kernel invo-
cation x starts or ends. A time measured from tau.start(x)
or tau.end(x) constrains only the cycle distance from event
x while leaving the exact cycle of x for the compiler to choose,
as the accumulation pin and the final loop of Figure 3 do.
4.2
Pinning a Time
A pin, written with the .at method, fixes the time at which
one operation or kernel invocation executes. Written on a
value, x.at(p) states that the operation producing 𝑥issues
at time 𝑝, while its result reaches its consumers after the
delays of Equation 1. The compiler chooses the issue cycle
of an operation without .at, subject to the time map of
an enclosing domain. A pin’s time expression may include
architectural latency constants queried via arch_int, such
as DOT in the accumulation pin of Figure 3.
Written on a call, k(...).at(p) sets the tau.T of callee
𝑘to the caller’s time 𝑝, which serves as the call’s invocation
time and shifts every explicit time in the callee by 𝑝. The
tau.T of the entry kernel is the start of the program. If
a callee contains no explicit times, its body starts at the
invocation time.
4.3
Iteration Domains
tau.domain schedules a loop by declaring an iteration space
together with a time map (at=lambda ...) from loop indices
to the start of each iteration. In polyhedral terms, a time
map defines an affine schedule from the iteration space to
cycle time [10], where the coefficient of a loop index sets the
initiation interval along that axis in modulo scheduling [35].
The earliest unpinned operation of each iteration initiates
the iteration at the exact cycle specified by the time map, and
every other unpinned operation in the loop body issues at
or after that cycle. An unpinned call takes its iteration start
as its invocation time. Binding a domain to a name, such as
tiles in Figure 3, lets the program refer to its iteration starts,
so tiles[k] is the start of iteration 𝑘and tau.end(tiles)
is the end of the domain. When a domain is written without
at, it declares only the bounds and the compiler chooses the
initiation interval of the loop.
Because a time map can reference any enclosing loop
index, a domain nested inside an untimed range loop can
incorporate the outer index into its schedule. In the softmax
pass of Figure 5, the term k*EXP_TILE_II in the time map
(➊) starts each key tile’s domain EXP_TILE_II cycles after
the previous one, which schedules the outer loop without a
separate time map.
5
TauIR
The compiler lowers explicit times from the DSL into at-
tributes of TauIR, the intermediate representation of TauLang.
This section describes how TauIR composes and lowers these
timing attributes onto a shared timeline and how affine time
validation rejects inconsistent schedules before placement
and scheduling.
5.1
Timing Attributes
TauIR represents each explicit time as one of three sym-
bolic affine timing attributes in MLIR [21] (Figure 6). A
call carries an invocation_time, a timed loop carries a
start_time map over its loop indices, and an operation
carries an issue_time pin. TauIR carries no unroll factor or
pipeline stage count, so these attributes capture the entire
programmer-specified schedule.
At the operation level, TauIR distinguishes explicit and
derived pins, each measured from a symbolic root. A pin
the programmer writes with .at is an explicit pin, which
fixes the exact cycle (from tau.T) or cycle distance (from
tau.start or tau.end) at which the operation issues. Every
unpinned operation inside a tau.domain instead carries a
derived pin, the time derived from the iteration start of its
nearest enclosing timed domain, which the operation takes
as a lower bound on its issue cycle. Among these operations,
only those with no intra-iteration operands, such as a load,
can issue first, so TauIR marks them as candidates to initiate
the iteration. The earliest scheduled candidate initiates the
iteration at the exact cycle of its derived pin. Each iteration
thus starts at the cycle specified by the time map without
requiring the programmer to pin an operation by hand. Vali-
dation and cluster partitioning rely on these operations for
exact cycle gaps across iterations. An unpinned operation

TauLang lowers these timing attributes onto a single time-
line in three stages while preserving their meaning. First,
it composes every call into the entry kernel by adding the
call’s invocation_time to every time attribute of the callee,
which places all times of the program on one shared timeline.
Second, for each unpinned operation inside a tau.domain,
it walks outward to the nearest enclosing timed domain to
attach its derived pin and marks the candidate operations
that can initiate each iteration. Finally, it unrolls the inner
loops of every loop nest, while each loop that stays rolled
takes the coefficient of its index in the pins as its initiation
interval. Each unrolled instance retains the source form of
its time attribute, so any diagnostic on a lowered operation
quotes the line the programmer wrote.
5.2
Affine Time Validation
As illustrated by the read-before-write bug in §2.4, explicit
times may conflict with machine latencies or with one an-
other. Before placement and scheduling run, TauLang checks
the explicit times algebraically on TauIR against necessary
timing conditions that hold regardless of slice placement and
leaves conflicts that depend on exact hop counts to place-
ment and scheduling. These conditions are independent of
placement because the explicit times, the dependence graph,
and the opcode latencies (𝑑func,𝑑skew) are already fixed in
TauIR, whereas placement only varies hop counts within
chip bounds. Each check takes the difference of two times
sharing a root and verifies that it satisfies these necessary
bounds across all loop indices. Validation rejects three error
patterns, namely (1) a conflict among explicit times, such as
a pin (.at) that places an operation before its iteration starts,
(2) an unbalanced pipeline in which reconvergent data paths
have different cycle lengths, and (3) a data-dependence vio-
lation in storage, such as reading before a write commits or
overwriting a value before it is read, which silently produces
wrong data.
Figure 7 traces the third pattern on the overlapped final
loop of §2.4. On the composed timeline, each read of 𝑆in the
final loop (at 𝑡𝑟, which initiates its iteration) must follow the
last write to that element in tile (𝑛, KB −1) (at 𝑡𝑠≥row start
+𝑊, where𝑊is the minimum load-to-store latency through
a row). This requires the upper bound 𝑃−𝐿−𝑊−𝑛(KB ·𝑃−
𝑀·II) of 𝑡𝑟−𝑡𝑠to remain non-negative. Because the final loop
drains columns faster than the walk finishes them (Figure 7b),
𝑡𝑟−𝑡𝑠< 0 from 𝑛= 1 through 𝑛= NB−1. Validation catches
this negative slack and reports the offending source lines
(Figure 7a). Starting column 𝑛at tiles[n + 1, 0] cancels
the term in 𝑛and leaves the bound 𝑃−𝐿−𝑊, so validation
accepts the program when 𝑃≥𝐿+𝑊(Figure 7c).
6
Space-Time Scheduling
Once affine time validation accepts the explicit times, the
compiler must still decide where and when every operation
runs. Placement assigns each operation to a slice, and sched-
uling assigns its issue cycle. Both choices must satisfy Equa-
tion 1 as well as the per-cycle bandwidth limits of SR tracks
and memory banks. Because values on a stream advance one
slice per cycle without waiting, placement and scheduling
are coupled through the hop count 𝛿in Equation 1. TauLang
satisfies these constraints in one of two flows, which trade
compile time against schedule quality. The space-first flow
decides placement and then scheduling, whereas the cluster
flow decides tensor placement and scheduling together in
an ILP.
6.1
Space-First Scheduling
In a tensor kernel, regular data and computation patterns
allow simple rules to assign every tensor to memory slices

and words and each operation to a matching functional slice
without search. Fixing these slice locations turns every hop
count 𝛿in Equation 1 into a known constant and decouples
scheduling from placement. To exploit this property for fast
compilation, the space-first flow runs rule-based placement
first and then schedules operations in cycle order with a
greedy list scheduler [11], prioritizing operations by their
critical-path latency to the end of the kernel.
For each loop, the scheduler builds a single-iteration sched-
ule at either the programmer-specified initiation interval or
the smallest interval at which no two iterations collide on
a slice. Repeating this schedule across the loop bounds ad-
vances the timeline to the end of the last iteration, so the
next loop or operation starts only after the loop drains. The
scheduler requires every operation pinned with .at to is-
sue at its written cycle and reports the source line of any
mismatch. While the space-first flow is fast and determin-
istic and serves as our baseline, separating placement from
loop-by-loop scheduling limits schedule quality. Because
hop counts 𝛿are fixed upfront, the list scheduler cannot
relocate slices to align operand arrival cycles, which forces
longer initiation intervals, while draining each loop prevents
cross-loop overlap.
6.2
Time-Guided Cluster Scheduling
Because placement and scheduling constrain each other, de-
ciding both together finds schedules that no fixed placement
allows, at the cost of a search space that grows exponentially
in the number of operations. In the cluster flow, TauLang
formulates this joint search as an ILP that decides which
memory slices hold each tensor buffer and when every oper-
ation issues. To keep the search tractable, as previewed in
§2.5, TauLang uses stream dependences and explicit times
to merge connected operations into timing clusters, whose
operations shift in time together (Figure 8b).
Placement. Most of the spatial freedom lies in the memory
slices, which far outnumber the vector, switch, and matrix
slices. How tensors are laid out across memory slices matters
most for performance, because it sets the hop count 𝛿that
each value travels along SR tracks to reach its consumer. The
ILP therefore keeps the functional slices from the rule-based
placement of the space-first flow and places only the tensor
buffers. A tensor buffer occupies consecutive memory slices
starting from a single base slice, and each memory access
runs on the slice that holds the part of the tensor it addresses.
The ILP thus carries one slice decision per buffer rather than
one per access.
Dependences. How a dependence constrains the schedule
depends on the storage or communication medium it tra-
verses (Figure 8a). A dependence through memory banks or
matrix weight planes is an inequality, because storage holds
a value across cycles until another write overwrites it. The
consumer may therefore read the value at any cycle after
the write commits. In contrast, a stream carries each value
from its producer to its consumer without waiting, so their
issue cycles must obey the rendezvous equality of Equation 1.
This equality is where placement and scheduling constrain
each other. Choosing the two slices fixes the hop count 𝛿and
therefore the cycle gap between the two operations. Con-
versely, once the two issue cycles are fixed, Equation 1 fixes
the hop count 𝛿between their slices.
Explicit times. Explicit times also state equalities between
issue cycles (red arrows in Figure 8b). A time map fixes the
issue cycle of the operation that initiates each iteration, and a
pin (.at) fixes the issue cycle of the pinned operation. Every
time map and pin therefore fixes the exact cycle gap between
an operation and its root.
Cluster partitioning. Given the operation DAG annotated
with dependence bounds and explicit times, the issue cycles
of its operations are not independent, because every exact
gap (=) fixes the cycle difference between two operations
before the solver runs. To presolve these equalities, TauLang
partitions the DAG along all exact-gap edges, from both
stream dependences and explicit times, into connected com-
ponents (timing clusters). Because operations in the same
cluster have fixed cycle offsets from one another, TauLang
substitutes out their individual issue cycles along a spanning
tree, which leaves at most one unknown start cycle per clus-
ter and none at all for the cluster rooted at tau.T. Their slice
placements are not independent either. When two stream-
connected operations fall into the same cluster, the cluster’s
start cycle cancels in Equation 1 and fixes the hop count 𝛿
between them, so placing one slice directly determines the
other at distance 𝛿.
Figure 8 illustrates this presolve on the row loop of tile
from §2.3 (Figure 3). In the original DAG (Figure 8a), machine
latencies give each edge either an exact gap (solid) or a mini-
mum gap (dashed). Because add takes two stream operands
that must reach VXM in the same cycle, ACC fixes when both

add and load S issue and joins the three operations with
exact gaps within each iteration. In contrast, ABC reads its
weights from a weight plane and takes only load A as a
stream input, while the remaining edges pass through the
matrix accumulator or memory and therefore impose only
minimum gaps on load A, load weight B, and store. In
Figure 8b, explicit times (red) add the missing exact gaps.
The time map of the row domain links load A across iter-
ations at interval II, and the .at on the accumulation fixes
ACC at 𝐻+ DOT cycles after load A. Because 𝐻is the hop
count from load A to ABC, ABC has no slack between load
A and ACC. Since load A initiates each iteration from tau.T,
partitioning merges all blue operations across iterations into
a single cluster with known issue cycles, so the solver sched-
ules only load weight B and store. From the fixed cycle
gaps inside this blue cluster, Equation 1 also determines the
hop counts from load A to ABC (𝐻hops) and from load S to
add, so the memory slices of 𝐴and 𝑆follow directly from the
matrix and vector slices. The pin on exp_f32 in §2.5 forms
its cluster the same way.
Resources. While cluster partitioning fixes cycle offsets
within each cluster, operations in different clusters can still
share a slice and must not collide on the same cycle or unit
occupancy. Rather than unrolling a loop into one variable
per iteration, the ILP keeps a single start-cycle variable for
each rolled operation and forbids start-cycle differences at
which two operations on the same slice would collide [35].
For example, if operations 𝐴and 𝐵each run three times at
a four-cycle interval (𝑎,𝑎+ 4,𝑎+ 8 and 𝑏,𝑏+ 4,𝑏+ 8), they
collide on a shared slice whenever 𝑎−𝑏∈{−8, −4, 0, 4, 8}.
Before solving, TauLang precomputes this forbidden set for
every pair of operations that may share a slice.
Objective and diagnostics. The ILP objective minimizes
the kernel makespan, defined as the cycle by which every
operation completes. TauLang solves the remaining slice
and issue-cycle variables with CP-SAT [32] under a fixed
time budget. When no valid schedule satisfies the explicit
times, TauLang reports the violated pins or the stream de-
pendence whose rendezvous Equation 1 cannot satisfy under
any placement.
7
Implementation
We implement TauLang in about 44K lines of Python and C++
on top of MLIR [21]. A Python front end lowers kernels into
our MLIR compiler pipeline, which carries symbolic timing
attributes through call composition, affine time validation,
and scheduling. We implement the ILP of the cluster flow
on top of the CP-SAT solver in OR-Tools [32]. Once slices
and issue cycles are assigned, backend passes allocate inter-
slice SR tracks, partition the program into one timestamped
instruction stream per slice, and assemble the streams into a
binary.
Finally, we implement a cycle-accurate software simulator
and a SystemVerilog RTL model of the machine’s control
logic. The simulator executes compiled binaries cycle by cy-
cle across all slices, computes every data value, and traps on
any rendezvous or resource violation, while the RTL model
validates the simulator’s cycle timing.
8
Evaluation
Our evaluation answers five questions that progress from
untimed compilation to explicit timing in TauLang. (1) How
much does deciding placement and issue cycles together
reduce schedule latency over space-first scheduling on un-
timed kernels (§8.2)? (2) Does fixing placement upfront still
lose optimality under an exact scheduler, and what domi-
nates the joint search cost (§8.3)? (3) Which explicit times
accelerate joint search without increasing schedule latency
(§8.4)? (4) How well do explicit time pins scale joint search
as kernel size grows (§8.5)? (5) How do parameterized time
maps let the programmer explore schedule trade-offs without
rewriting the kernel (§8.6)?
8.1
Evaluation Setup
Metrics. We report kernel latency in execution cycles and
compile time in wall-clock seconds. On a statically scheduled
machine, the binary fixes the slice and issue cycle of every
instruction and each opcode has a fixed, data-independent la-
tency, so a single run determines a kernel’s exact cycle count
and small problem sizes suffice to validate the simulator
against RTL. We measure all kernels on our cycle-accurate
simulator, whose instruction latencies and issue intervals
come from our 93-slice SystemVerilog RTL and match the
published TSP parameters [2]. Since full RTL simulation in
Verilator is too slow for larger problem sizes, we run the
smallest instance of each kernel and one ResNet residual
block in Verilator under both flows and confirm that the RTL
matches the simulator’s cycle count on every binary without
timing or resource violations.
Configurations. We compare the two scheduling flows of
TauLang. The baseline space-first flow fixes slice placement
first and runs a greedy list scheduler (§6.1), whereas the
cluster flow runs joint search, solving the ILP of §6.2 with
CP-SAT [32] under a 60-second budget per solve. The case
study raises this budget to 100 seconds, and to 600 seconds
for some pairs near its front.
Workloads. We evaluate ten kernels spanning BLAS [22],
PolyBench [33], ResNet [14], and Transformer layers [38, 40]
(Table 1). Each kernel is evaluated at three problem sizes (30
instances in total) across three DSL versions. The untimed
version writes no explicit times, the time maps version re-
places range loops with tau.domain and its time map, and
the pins version adds one to three lines of .at. Sections 8.2
and 8.3 compile the untimed version in both flows to isolate
the effect of joint placement and scheduling. Section 8.4 then

8.2
Deciding Placement and Cycles Together
On a statically scheduled machine, placement and scheduling
are coupled through stream hop counts (Equation 1). We
first test whether deciding both together is necessary for
schedule quality by comparing the cluster flow against the
space-first flow across all 30 untimed kernel instances. As
shown in Figure 9, the cluster flow finds a lower-latency
schedule than the space-first flow on every instance and
achieves a 1.40× geometric-mean speedup (ranging from
1.04× to 2.22×). Three repeated compiles of each instance
produce identical latency.
Two mechanisms explain the gain. First, choosing memory
placement together with issue cycles shortens loop initiation
intervals. Because the space-first flow fixes tensor place-
ments before scheduling, operands streaming from different
memory slices incur mismatched hop counts 𝛿, which forces
the greedy list scheduler to pad the initiation interval to
avoid collisions. By placing memory buffers to align operand

Figure 10. Solve time (bars, left axis, percentage) and latency
(marks, right axis, ratio) of the fixed-placement flow relative
to the untimed cluster flow. Bar colors and marker shapes

for at least one size. AXPY matches the optimal untimed

arrival cycles, the cluster flow reduces the initiation interval
at the largest problem size from 19 cycles to 1 on Softmax,
from 12 to 1 on RMSNorm, and from 4 to 1 on AXPY, so
their speedups grow with the number of rows or vectors.
Second, joint search overlaps consecutive loops. On GEMM
and Conv2D, both flows achieve a 1-cycle initiation interval
within each loop, but the space-first flow drains each loop
completely before starting the next. In contrast, the cluster
flow schedules all loops together and overlaps each weight
install with the tail of the rows streaming through the previ-
ous weight plane, which reduces the interval between the
four weight installs of 4-block GEMM from 170–178 cycles
to 84 cycles.
Across all ten kernels, the speedup of joint search grows
with problem size wherever the cycles it saves recur in every
iteration or block, as in AXPY, Softmax, RMSNorm, GEMM,
and Horner. Conversely, the speedups of GEMV, MLP, and
Jacobi-2D stay nearly flat because fixed setup or serialized
SXM shifts dominate their latency, while MaxPool peaks at
the smallest size where its short loop allows tighter output
spacing.
8.3
Placement Ablation
Because space-first scheduling both fixes placement upfront
and uses a greedy list scheduler, §8.2 alone does not show
whether fixing placement still loses optimality under an exact
scheduler. To isolate the effect of fixed placement, we evalu-
ate a fixed-placement flow that solves the same untimed ILP
while holding every buffer at the slice chosen by the space-
first flow’s rule-based placement. As shown in Figure 10, even

mal for its given placement, fixed placement still increases
latency across all 30 instances by 1.24× in geometric mean
(ranging from 1.02× to 1.92×) compared to the cluster flow,
which factors the 1.40× speedup of §8.2 into 1.13× from the
ILP scheduler and 1.24× from joint placement. While the
fixed-placement ILP still overlaps consecutive loops, CP-SAT
proves that the 1-cycle initiation intervals reached by the
cluster flow are infeasible under the rule-based placement
on 19 of the 30 instances, so the minimum interval at the
largest size rises to 2 cycles on Softmax, 8 on RMSNorm, and
4 on AXPY. At the same time, fixed placement cuts solve
time to at most 2.4 seconds per instance, or 0.01% to 4.4%
of the cluster flow’s solve time, which shows that searching
memory slice placements accounts for over 95% of the solve
time.
8.4
Choosing What to Pin
While joint search is necessary for schedule quality, search-
ing memory slice placements and issue cycles together is
costly. To accelerate this search without raising latency, a
TauLang program can specify either loop initiation inter-
vals via time maps or operation cycle offsets via explicit
time pins. Using the machine latencies exposed by TauLang,
our kernels each pin one to three recurring pipeline offsets
with known optimal values, such as the accumulation after
a matrix multiply or the interval between weight installs.
Figure 11 compares the time maps and pins versions against
the untimed version (median compile time of three runs).
Explicit time pins cut compile time by 1.72× in geometric
mean and by up to 3.50× on AXPY, while matching the un-
timed latency on 28 of the 30 instances and staying within
one cycle of it on 8- and 16-row Jacobi-2D. Time maps alone,

by contrast, leave compile time unchanged (1.00× geometric
mean), because they fix only the initiation interval, which
the solver already finds in its first search round. They also
raise the latency of Jacobi-2D to 1.01×, because its time map
starts the sum loop only after every shift loop finishes.
Pins shorten the search for memory slice placements,
which dominates solve time. Pinning the issue cycles at
both ends of a stream dependence fixes the hop count 𝛿
between their slices through Equation 1, which prunes can-
didate placements. The compile-time benefit therefore de-
pends on how much placement search the pinned timing
relation removes. Consequently, kernels with more irregular
data layouts, such as AXPY, Softmax, and GEMV, gain the
largest compile-time speedups. Because these layouts cre-
ate many candidate placements for the untimed solver to
compare, fixing their pipeline gaps with pins cuts compile
time by 2.79× to 3.50×. In contrast, MLP and GEMM carry
the same weight-to-accumulation pin as GEMV, but each
phase repeats a uniform data layout, which yields smaller
compile-time speedups of 1.00× and 1.45×. Beyond cutting
compile time at these sizes, pruning candidate placements
also changes how the search scales with kernel size.
8.5
Scaling Joint Search
To test whether pins let the cluster flow scale, we grow two
representative workloads far past the sizes of Table 1. First,
we scale 16-row GEMM from 2 to 1,636 blocks of 𝐾, where
each block adds a weight-install phase followed by a row-
streaming phase. Second, we stack 8-row ResNet residual
blocks [14], each fusing two 3×3 convolutions and a skip
connection. In both, all blocks are fused into one kernel
whose weights and intermediate buffers must fit on the chip
together, so the compiler must place and schedule all phases
globally.
We compile each workload both untimed and with pins,
plus one pin between consecutive convolutions in ResNet,
10


--- Page 11 ---
TauLang: A Language and Compiler for Space-Time Programming on Statically Scheduled Accelerators
while the solver still places every buffer and weight set and
schedules all unpinned operations. Figure 12 plots the total
solve time per compile (averaged over three compiles) as
kernel size grows. We plot solve time rather than compile
time because building the ILP takes the same time in both
versions wherever both find a schedule. The untimed solver
stops scaling early. Untimed GEMM solve time grows by
10.5× from 2 to 16 blocks and finds no schedule within the
budget at 32 blocks, while untimed ResNet reaches the budget
at 4 residual blocks and finds no schedule at 8.
With pins, by contrast, the solver finds schedules at far
larger sizes, and its solve time grows sub-linearly with kernel
size. As GEMM grows 818× (from 2 to 1,636 blocks), solve
time grows by only 97× (from 0.63 to 61 seconds, staying
near 20 seconds between 256 and 512 blocks), and as ResNet
grows 128× (from 1 to 128 residual blocks), solve time grows
by only 38× (from 1.1 to 42 seconds, with no schedule at 256
blocks). Every completed solve proves its schedule optimal
under its pins. Across the sizes where the untimed solver
succeeds, pins reduce solve time by 4.5× to 15.5× with zero
latency penalty and match the exact untimed growth rate of
96 cycles per 𝐾-block in GEMM and 648 cycles per residual
block in ResNet. On 8-block ResNet, the single pin between
consecutive convolutions cuts solve time by a further 3.3×
over intra-convolution pins alone (from 14.9 to 4.5 seconds).
Once timing clusters tame the search itself, scaling to these
sizes exposes the next largest cost in compile time, which
is building the ILP before the solver runs. Building the ILP
involves no search, as it only precomputes the forbidden
start-cycle differences across operation pairs that may share
a slice. This step takes under one second up to 64 GEMM
blocks and 8 residual blocks, and reaches 182 and 194 seconds
at the largest sizes, 3.0× and 4.6× as long as the solve. Overall,
a few pins in TauLang let the solver prove schedules optimal
under those pins at 1,636 GEMM blocks and 128 residual
blocks, far beyond the sizes the untimed solver reaches.
8.6
Exploring Schedules by Parameters
Although time maps alone do not accelerate solver search, pa-
rameterizing their strides lets the programmer explore sched-
ule trade-offs on the same kernel, as in the GEMM schedules
of Figure 4. We demonstrate this on a flow-matching ac-
tion head that refines a chunk of 𝑁= 50 robot actions over
𝐾= 10 sequential Euler steps, following 𝜋0 [5]. Reactive
control minimizes first-item latency so the robot acts on the
earliest action [15, 19], whereas chunked execution mini-
mizes whole-output time across the full chunk [6]. Because
the kernel omits cross-item attention, its 50 items execute
independently, while within each item step 𝑘+ 1 depends
on the two matrix projections and Euler update of step 𝑘.
A single 2D time map, tau.T + a*II + k*STEP, schedules
step 𝑘of item 𝑎, spacing successive items by II cycles and
successive steps of the same item by STEP cycles. Only these
two stride parameters change across compiles. Reducing

Pareto front
Figure 13. Exploring the trade-off between first-item latency
and whole-output time on a single kernel. Each circle is a
compiled schedule for a parameter pair (II, STEP) at 𝑁= 50
and 𝐾= 10, and the solid line connects the Pareto front of
the compiled pairs. The right panel enlarges the front inside
the dashed region and labels each front schedule with its
(II, STEP) values.
STEP lowers first-item latency because the final step of the
first item starts (𝐾−1) · STEP cycles after its first, whereas
reducing II lowers whole-output time because the last item
starts (𝑁−1) · II cycles after the first.
We first screen 891 parameter pairs across II from 16 to 48
cycles and STEP from 274 to 300 cycles. Before invoking the
solver, affine time validation rejects 407 of these pairs within
about a second each, because their strides assign two matrix
operations to the same slice in the same cycle. A compile
that finds a schedule takes 32 to 518 seconds (median 68), so
we solve 84 of the 484 accepted pairs on a coarse grid of II
from 20 to 48 with six STEP values and sample 30 more pairs
around the grid’s front (II down to 13, STEP up to 311). Of
these 114 pairs, 44 yield a schedule and 70 reach the budget,
mostly at tighter strides where a larger budget could expand
the front further.
Eight of the 44 schedules form the Pareto front among
compiled pairs in Figure 13. Along the front, II falls from
29 to 14 cycles while STEP rises from 277 to 303. Reactive
control selects (29, 277), which lowers first-item latency by
237 cycles compared to (14, 303) (2839 versus 3076 cycles),
whereas chunked execution selects (14, 303), which reduces
whole-output time by 498 cycles (3762 versus 4260 cycles).
Across all 44 schedules, whole-output time exceeds first-item
latency by exactly 49 · II cycles, and first-item latency falls
between 9·STEP +346 and 9·STEP +360 cycles. The program-
mer can thus predict both latencies from (II, STEP) to within
14 cycles before compiling, while the compiler determines
which pairs are realizable. Adapting the kernel between con-
trol regimes requires only changing two parameter values
rather than rewriting the kernel.

9
Related Work
Tile-level kernel languages. Triton [37], TileLang [39],
CuTile [4], Tilus [7], Helion [26], and Gluon [30] let a pro-
grammer express block-level computation over tiles while
the compiler chooses layouts, warps, and pipelines. TauLang
retains this tile-level programming model of loads, stores,
matrix multiplies, and epilogues, but adds first-class cycle
times so the compiler can statically schedule targets that
lack dynamic hardware synchronization. While Exo [18]
also exposes scheduling to the programmer through explicit
rewrites, its schedules specify operation orderings rather
than issue cycles.
Timing in hardware languages. High-level hardware de-
sign languages such as Spatial [20], Dahlia [27], and Aether-
ling [8] raise accelerator design above the register-transfer
level while leaving cycle timing to the compiler. Closer to
our philosophy, Filament [28] and Lilac [29] embed cycle in-
tervals into the type system to verify hardware pipelines stat-
ically. However, because these languages synthesize custom
circuits, the designer can insert registers or buffers whenever
a path needs delay. In contrast, TauLang targets a fixed ac-
celerator with predetermined latencies, so it satisfies explicit
times by scheduling operations jointly with tensor placement
across memory slices.
Compilers for spatial accelerators. TileLoom [23] simi-
larly compiles tile programs to spatial accelerators by plan-
ning tile placement and data movement, but its schedule
stops at spatial assignment and execution order. CGRA com-
pilers assign both spatial units and modulo cycles [24, 25, 35],
often using integer programming [16, 31]. However, because
CGRAs buffer early operands in local registers, data depen-
dences only bound consumer issue cycles from below. On our
target, stream operands obey the exact rendezvous equality
of Equation 1, which TauLang combines with programmer-
written explicit times to merge operations into timing clus-
ters before solving.
Polyhedral scheduling. Polyhedral compilers represent
loop schedules as affine functions of the iteration indices
and derive them automatically over data dependences [10].
TauLang adopts this affine representation for its domain time
maps, but lets the programmer write the schedule directly as
cycle times while the compiler validates dependences alge-
braically. Whereas traditional polyhedral schedules specify
logical ordering for dynamically synchronized hardware,
Clockwork [17] interprets affine schedules as physical cycles
to synthesize and size buffers for image-processing hard-
ware. In TauLang, time maps likewise denote exact cycles,
but because the target hardware is fixed, a valid schedule
must satisfy Equation 1 across existing slices and memory
banks.
10
Conclusion
TauLang is, to our knowledge, the first kernel language
and compiler for statically scheduled accelerators. By mak-
ing cycle time a first-class, parameterized language con-
struct, TauLang decouples a kernel’s schedule from its code
structure and enables whole-program schedule exploration
without rewriting code. Lowering explicit times into TauIR
lets the compiler validate timing algebraically before search
and merge connected operations into timing clusters dur-
ing joint space-time scheduling. Across our benchmarks, a
few explicit time pins accelerate joint search and scale it to
thousand-block kernels while matching untimed schedule
latency within a single cycle.
